zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical reference consulted after independent scan reading: NINJAL, *Entry Words Data of Nippojisho*, version 202510, developed by Hideyuki Ohshima with assistance from Taichi Aida ([official release](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html)), licensed under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). This review’s transcription corrections and explanatory notes are distinct from the supplied dataset.

lines.note: Continues the preceding page’s adverb of respect: speaking respectfully, or remaining in a respectful posture. The scan separates the alternative marker l from iru; OCR Iiru incorrectly fused them. The opening paragraph mark is visible.
Completes the Portuguese alternatives: to be with reverence and humility. The word is humildade, not OCR humaldade; the gloss explains the manner of both Japanese verbs above.

runs.text: O vigiar toda a noite na

lines.note: Tsuya is an all-night vigil; yomosugara supplies the Japanese explanation “throughout the night.” The Portuguese begins the description of keeping watch in a place of worship.

The vigil takes place in a varela or church. The example means performing a vigil, with an alternative verb below. Tcuyauo is retained as printed: no secure cedilla is visible in this occurrence, although the headword has one.

Moosu completes the alternative expression for holding a vigil. The Portuguese describes spending the night at a tera or hermitage; Tera is a Japanese term embedded in that explanation and appears upright.
Vigiando completes the preceding sentence: the night is spent keeping vigil. This short continuation is a full physical body row.

Tsuyatsuya is introduced as an adverb, with its negative-verb usage explained below. The second c is visibly uncedilled, so printed Tçuyatcuya is retained. After independent scan reading, the bundled NINJAL index (251c02; Ohshima and Aida, version 202510, CC BY 4.0; [release](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html)) corroborates this spelling and explicitly notes the likely printing error; it is not silently corrected.

runs.text: mente por elegancia, & com verbos negatiuos

lines.note: Completes commummente and specifies elegant usage with negative verbs. The scan supports verbos, replacing OCR verhos; this grammatical restriction explains the following negative example.
The adverb is used for matters of consideration or importance. Vt introduces tsuyatsuya across the line break; conſideração has no internal word division.
Completes tsuyatsuya henji wo moosazu, giving no reply at all. The Portuguese reſpondendo ends in o, not OCR e; the final nada follows on the next line.
Nada completes “not answering anything.” The negative meaning belongs with tsuyatsuya and moosazu on the preceding rows.
Tsuyashi, tsuyasu, tsuyaita means wasting or squandering. The historical -aita principal part is retained, and Taca- begins takara in the next line’s example.
Takara wo tsuyasu means squandering one’s wealth. Mal, not OCR mol, is visible. The printed geſtar is retained rather than normalized to gastar from the surrounding sense.
Fazenda completes the wealth example. The next expression, kokka wo tsuyasu, extends the verb figuratively to ruining a realm and its houses.
The Portuguese gloss explains the figurative example as ruining the kingdom and households. The capital in Reino and the printed Desbaratar are preserved.
Tsue is a staff or rod. The example tsue wo atsuru begins here and continues on the next row, with the printed hyphen after a.

runs.text: Dar açoutes, ou pancadas cõ vara, &c.

lines.note: Atsuru completes the example of striking with a rod. The gloss specifies lashes or blows; cõ retains its abbreviation mark rather than being expanded to com.
The intransitive tsuye, tsuyuru, tsuyeta concerns being wasted or expended. The Portuguese reflexive verbs distinguish it from the preceding transitive tsuyasu entry.
Something is spent badly; takara ga tsuyuru makes the wealth itself the subject. The example is an intransitive counterpart of takara wo tsuyasu above.
The first sentence translates the waste of wealth. A new example, haremono ga tsuyeta, begins the sense of a swelling breaking open and is divided after tçu-.
Yeta completes tsuyeta, equated with tsubureta: the swelling burst. The Portuguese name of the abscess or tumour begins leicẽ- and is continued on the next physical row.

runs.text: ſo, ou inchaço. ¶ Item, Desmancharſe, ou

lines.note: Completes leicẽſo and adds inchaço, a swelling. A further sense begins with falling apart; it continues into walls and ground on the following rows.

runs.text: cair a parede, ou arruinar a terra. Vt,

lines.note: The verb also describes a wall falling or the ground collapsing. Ixi- begins ishigaki, the stone-wall subject of the example.
Ishigaki, alternatively kishi, ga tsuyeta describes collapse of a stone wall or bank. The printed separation after caqi is retained; the Portuguese parede is divided across rows.

runs.text: de de pedra, ou arruinou a terra, barroca, &c.

lines.note: Completes the explanation: the stone wall fell, or the earth or bank collapsed. Barroca belongs to the terrain description, not another Japanese expression.

The noun tsuye is equated with shitsui and glossed as expenditure or expenses. The anomalous printed-looking deſſeſas is retained from the aligned baseline: enlargement does not securely establish the p of expected despesas, and same-page p types have a distinct bowl. The tall middle types remain a nonblocking graphic uncertainty.
Tsue yari is a short spear resembling a staff. The following lines describe its concealed upper blade and staff-like lower fitting.

runs.text: que tẽ o ferro ẽ baixo como de bordão, & o de

lines.note: The lower iron fitting resembles that of a staff; the upper one is described next. The complete second pass and enlargement reveal a tilde in tẽ; both tẽ and ẽ are retained without expansion. Como has no secure tilde despite the OCR’s cõmo.

runs.text: cima como de lãça curta cuberto cõ hũa bainha.

lines.note: The upper fitting is like a short spear’s blade, covered with a sheath. The abbreviation marks in lãça, cõ, and hũa remain unexpanded.

Tsuuyoo is explained by itami kayugaru: suffering pain and itching. Both long-vowel marks are carons on enlargement; the abraded u itself is partly lost. This corrects the OCR circumflex over u without conflating the final caron with the next entry’s circumflex.
Mechão completes comechão, itching. The closing S is upright and labels written usage; it is not part of the italic Portuguese word.
The next tsuuyoo entry concerns communication, dealings, and commerce. Its final circumflex contrasts visibly with the preceding pain-and-itching entry’s caron; the two are not harmonized.

Completes commercio and begins an example of intercourse from Nagasaki to Arima. The damaged final syllable is tçǔ-, continuing into yô below; its upright u and long-vowel mark replace the OCR’s spurious italic è.
Completes tsuuyoo suru, maintaining dealings or communication. The Portuguese describes the same connection and divides deſde across the physical rows.
Completes deſde and names the route from Nagasaki to Arima. The scan supports capital N rather than OCR R; the Portuguese spelling Nagaſaqui differs from Japanese Nagaſaqi above and is retained.
Tsuyoi means hard, firm, or strong, directly glossed rija and forte. The two short Japanese derivatives on the next line belong to this adjective.
Tsuyosa is the noun for strength, followed by the adverbial tsuyoo. The middle letters of Tçuyô are abraded; the remaining shapes and adjective-family context support y rather than OCR j.
Tsuyome, tsuyomuru, tsuyometa is the transitive verb to strengthen. Fazer is completed by forte on the next row.
Hito no kokoro wo tsuyomuru means strengthening someone’s heart or resolve. The heavily worn example is supported by surviving letters and the Portuguese explanation below.

runs.text: Esforçar, ou dar alento a alguem.

lines.note: The example means encouraging someone or giving them spirit. The printed Esforçar has a short s before f and is retained without a global long-s substitution.

runs.text: Força, & animo, ou couſa de valẽ

lines.note: Tsuyomi denotes strength, courage, or a feat of valour. Valẽ continues into tia below, but no clear terminal hyphen is supplied where the baseline has none.
Completes valentia. Hito no tsuyomi ni naru means becoming a source of strength for someone; the Portuguese begins for-taleza, with o rather than OCR e.
Completes fortaleza and the support-for-someone gloss. The following tsuyomi wo yuu or dasu example starts with the divided Tçuyo-.
Tsuyomi wo yuu, alternatively dasu, means speaking or showing oneself boldly. The Portuguese begins “speak with courage,” and continues with firmness below.

runs.text: fortaleza, ou moſtrar animo teſo, & conſ-

lines.note: Completes speaking with strength, then describes showing firm and constant spirit. The f in fortaleza has a cross-stroke; ou and the divided conſ- replace OCR cu and cenſ-.
Completes constante and adds that the person does not shrink or become abashed. The negative clause supplies the practical sense of the preceding display of courage.

Tsuyorakashi, tsuyorakasu, tsuyorakashita means to strengthen or make strong. Although this bottom row is worn, the complete Portuguese gloss is recoverable; the OCR’s mixed italic u and garbled Foitaleaer/iufazorſoris are not printed word forms.
Tsuyorashi is given the same strengthening sense as tsuyorakashi across the column boundary. Kokoro begins the example and is divided before its object particle on the next row.
Kokoro wo tsuyorasu means heartening or encouraging. The Portuguese animar and eſforçar explain the figurative sense of strengthening the heart.
Tsuyori is strength or support. The example tsuyori ni naru begins here and continues on the next physical line.

runs.text: Fazerſe, ou ficar forte com a

lines.note: Tsuyori ni naru means becoming or remaining strong through someone’s help. The scan separates com a; the helper is specified below.
Completes the explanation as strength gained with another person’s assistance. This short phrase belongs to the preceding noun example.
Tsuyori, tsuyoru, tsuyotta is the verb to grow strong or be strong. The Portuguese initial is F, not OCR T, as confirmed by its cross-stroke and strengthening sense.
Zen ga tsuyoreba, aku ga yowaru states that when virtue grows strong, vice weakens. Consonantal initial I in Ien represents the z/j-series value; it is not an error to modernize.

runs.text: do a virtude forte, os vicios enfraquecem.

lines.note: Completes Sendo and translates the moral comparison: with virtue strong, vices become weak. The plural Portuguese vicios is part of the explanatory rendering.
Tsuyoyumi first means a strong, stout bow; a second sense begins “a good…” and is completed as an archer below.
Frecheiro and forçoſo complete the second sense: a good, powerful archer. The historical frecheiro spelling is preserved rather than modernized.
Tsuyu means dew. Tsuyu ga oku describes dew lying or settling, and the Portuguese begins the corresponding state on leaves.

runs.text: o orualho ſobre as folhas das aruores, ou er-

lines.note: The dew rests on the leaves of trees or herbs. The terminal er- is visibly divided from uas on the next line.
Completes er-uas, then introduces tsuyu wo oku, a separate usage glossed as ornamenting food. The object-particle uo distinguishes it from dew settling in the preceding example.

runs.text: iguarias, ou comer que ſe poem na ne-

lines.note: The expression concerns delicacies or food set on the table. The expected word is mesa, but the visible divided fragment reads ne- and the aligned OCR agrees; retain that apparent damaged or anomalous form rather than supply an unsupported m. It continues as ſa below.

runs.text: ſa, ou em algũa caixa com folha de ouro, ou

lines.note: Completes the apparent ne- / ſa, understood in context as mesa, and describes garnishing food on a table or in a box with gold leaf. The scan supports folha, without the extra t of OCR foltha.
Silver leaf completes the ornamenting sense. Tsuyu wo utsu introduces sprinkling water; Botar, not OCR Betar, is supported by the rounded vowel and the gloss’s action.

runs.text: com a mão, ou cõ ramo por cima dalgũa couſa

lines.note: The water is scattered by hand or with a branch over something. The tilde in mão remains over a, while cõ and dalgũa retain their own printed marks.
The sprinkling refreshes or cools the object. Tsuyu no inochi, a life like dew, begins the next figurative expression; Vi- starts its Portuguese translation.

runs.text: da breue q̃ logo ſe acaba como orualho. ¶

lines.note: Vida breue explains a brief life that ends quickly like dew. Tçu begins another example on the following row; no new hyphen is supplied to its unhyphenated baseline fragment.
Tsuyu hodo mo zonjenu, alternatively itasanu, means not knowing or doing even the slightest amount. The printed period after l is retained, and the Portuguese begins the knowing alternative.

runs.text: ou não fazer nẽ hũ tamanino dalgũa couſa.

lines.note: Completes the negative alternatives: not doing even a tiny amount of something. Tamanino is retained as the printed diminutive form, without supplying an expected h.

runs.text: Chuuas grãdes, & continuadas q̃ ha em

lines.note: A separate tsuyu entry denotes the rainy season: heavy, continuous rains. Continuadas is worn across its latter half; surviving strokes and the grammatical phrase support this reading rather than the OCR’s broken con tinue dae.

The rains occur during a certain part of summer. The regional explanation gives Nagaxi in Ximo; both Japanese names are upright within the Portuguese sentence, rather than splitting Nagaxi between typefaces.
Tsuyukusa is described as a certain small herb. The short gloss supports the plant-name reading without requiring a modern botanical species identification.

runs.text: O ſair no principio do auto por

lines.note: Tsuyu harai denotes the performer who comes out at the beginning of a play. The theatrical sense develops the idea of an opening act, rather than literal dew-clearing here.

runs.text: primeira figura, & dizer algũa couſa. ¶ I-

lines.note: The first character appears and says something. Primeira corrects OCR primetra; I- begins the next Item and remains italic with the Portuguese apparatus.

runs.text: tem bailar, ou cantar como Mais, &c. no

lines.note: Completes Item and adds opening dance or song, with Mais naming the Japanese performance form within Portuguese prose. Its printed italic treatment is retained for human whole-word font review.

runs.text: principio como pera tomar o tom, ou aquietar

lines.note: The opening performance serves to establish the pitch or quiet the audience. Tomar o tom is the musical explanation, not another Japanese phrase.
Completes the audience explanation and gives tsuyu harai wo suru, performing this opening role. The final I- starts the italic Idem on the next line.

runs.text: dem. ¶ Itẽ, permet. Dar principio a algũa

lines.note: Completes Idem, then extends the expression figuratively to starting something. Algũa has a final a, not OCR s, agreeing with couſa on the following row.

runs.text: couſa como no beberete tomar primeiro o Sa-

lines.note: The figurative example is taking the sake cup first at a drinking gathering. Sa- begins the embedded Japanese vessel name Sacazzuqui, continued below; its printed italic styling is preserved.
Cazzuqui completes Sacazzuqui, the drinking cup used in the preceding example. This is a divided Japanese term embedded in the Portuguese explanation, not a separate headword.
Tsuuzu, alternatively tsuuji, means an interpreter. The marks over u are carons in this row; the alternative marker l remains separate from the Japanese forms.
Tsuzu denotes ports where vessels anchor or lie. Surgem has the maritime sense of coming to anchor, which explains the harbour gloss.

Another tsuzu is identified with the number ten. The phrase tsuzu hatachi introduces the age expression translated as twenty years on the next line; the numeral is read 10 rather than the OCR letter sequence 1o.
Tsuzu nijuu is offered as an alternative to tsuzu hatachi. The Portuguese explicitly gives twenty years of age; no conjectural arithmetic explanation is inserted into the source.

Tsuzumari is the contraction or shrinking verb, with shijimari preferred by the compiler. Both abbreviated continuations visibly give u here; they are preserved without adding an expected r. A detached round ink mark lies below and to the right of the final u; it remains visible in the crop and is not conjecturally assigned as punctuation.
The reflexive Portuguese verbs give the intransitive sense, becoming shorter or shrinking. They distinguish this entry from the following transitive one.
Tsuzume is the transitive counterpart, again with shijime recommended as the better form. Meliùs is italic editorial Latin; the Japanese alternative stays roman.
The meaning is to shorten or reduce. Shotai wo tsuzumuru begins the household-economy example, with a visible terminal hyphen rather than the OCR period after tçuz.
Completes tsuzumuru. The gloss specifies reducing the people and expenses of the household, a concrete economical application of the contraction verb.
Da caſa completes the phrase about a household’s members and expenditure. The short continuation is retained independently as a physical body row.
Tsuzumi is glossed as a small drum or tambour. The printed Tabaquinho is retained without supplying an unprinted m or imposing a modern instrument-name spelling.
Tsuzumuki denotes a challenge, fight, or wrestling encounter between two people. The numerical restriction follows on the next line.
Completes “between two,” then gives an example of two opponents striking one another. The printed qiriyǒta is retained as the historical form, with a caron over o.

runs.text: rirãoſe dous q̃ entre ſi ſem mais companhia pe-

lines.note: Completes Ferirãoſe: two people struck one another, without any additional company. The Portuguese verb pelejar is divided pe- / lejarão, and q̃ is not expanded.

Completes the description of fighting as in a duel or challenge. Deſafio has f, not the OCR’s second ſ. A new Japanese example begins with Tçuzzumuqini and continues beyond the page; the separate bottom catchword is not appended to this body row.

zones.label: Printed catchword
zones.note: The isolated lower-right word is page furniture. The following page is not included in this package.

lines.note: The isolated bottom-right catchword anticipates continuation of the final Japanese example. Its position and smaller detached setting distinguish it from body text; the next page has not been inspected here.
